text: From NPR News, this is ALL THINGS CONSIDERED. I'm Michele Norris.
And I'm Melissa Block.

Election 2006 ushers in a record number of women to both the House and the Senate. There will be two more women senators, both Democrats, to make a total of 16. In the House, there will be a net gain of at least three more congresswomen, up from 67 to at least 70 - several races are still undecided -and of course, Nancy Pelosi is poised to become the first woman speaker of the House.
Joining us to sort through what all this means is Debbie Walsh. She directs the Center for American Women and Politics at Rutgers University in New Jersey. Thanks for being with us.
Nice to be here.
Debbie, in a year when there was a solid Democratic sweep, would you have expected broader gains among women? Most of the women who were running were Democrats.

Well, what we did see was a story of party here, even in the women's races. While we do have 10 brand-new women who've been elected to the House, eight of those women were Democrats, and we saw no losses among the Democratic incumbent women, but we in fact did lose four Republican women from the House, and there's still some of these undecided races that involve Republican. So there's the potential to lose even more.
So it's a good news story for Democratic and a not so good news story for the Republican women.
In past years, some elections have been considered, or at least one has been considered the year of the woman. You wouldn't consider that the case this year?

Well, I think it's the year of the woman for different reasons this year. We saw in 1992, which was dubbed the year of the woman, we saw 19 new women coming into Congress, and I don't mean 19 new women, I actually mean a net gain of 19, which is far, far more than what we're seeing this year. So we haven't matched those numbers, but we have done, obviously, is we've attained a level of leadership within Congress that we have never attained before.
How do you see the impact of Nancy Pelosi, who is about to become by all measure the new speaker of the House?

Well, I think that what's terrific about hearing her now as she talks about her role as speaker is that she's not shying away from this question of - that she is the first woman. She's taking that on, and she's talking about the fact that this is sending a message to voters and to the general public that women can do anything. And she also talks about the fact that she wants to comport herself in such a way as the first woman speaker that it won't be long before there is another woman speaker.
There were a record number of women running for state legislative office this year. Is that were you would look to find women in the pipeline who might eventually end up in Congress?

Absolutely. If you look at the women who are currently serving in Congress, over half of them came out of state legislatures or county government. So yes, the pipeline is about moving up and through the system. I mean, one of the reasons we saw '92 as this, you know, stellar year was you had women who were already in elected positions, and when the opportunity of '92 came along with a tremendous number of open seats, a national focus on the problem of no women in the United States Senate on the Judiciary Committee when Anita Hill came to testify and it put a spotlight on that, you had women who were prepared to seize that opportunity.

So you need those women in the pipeline, and that pipeline has to keep flowing to make sure that there are more women in Congress, and when Nancy Pelosi steps down eventually as speaker of the House, that there are more women ready and waiting to rise to those kinds of high-level leadership positions.
Debbie Walsh, thank you very much.
Thank you.
Debbie Walsh directs the Center for American Women and Politics at Rutgers University in New Brunswick, New Jersey.
Now for a trivia question. Who were the first women to serve in the U.S. House and Senate?

On the House side, it was Montana Republican Jeannette Rankin. She was elected in 1916, 90 years ago this week. After serving one term, she declined re-nomination and instead ran unsuccessfully for a Senate seat.

That wasn't the end of Jeannette Rankin's political career, however. Two decades later, she ran again for the House and won on a staunch anti-war platform. Her pacifist views brought her fame and notoriety. She was the only person to have voted against U.S. entry into both world wars.

Now, the first female U.S. senator was Georgia Democrat Rebecca Felton. In a symbolic move, the 87-year-old Felton was appointed to fill a vacancy in the Senate. She took the oath of office on November 21, 1922 and served for just 24 hours.

Aside from her day in the Senate, Felton was a strong opponent of anti-lynching legislation. She made some unsavory remarks about blacks. But she did make this prediction during her time in the Senate chamber.

"When the women of the country come in and sit with you, I pledge you that you will get ability, you will get integrity of purpose, you will get exalted patriotism and you will get unstinted usefulness."

For more, I spoke with Debbie Walsh, director of the Center for American Women in Politics at Rutgers' Eagleton Institute of Politics. Walsh agrees that women have made steady political gains in years, but they're still a long way to go.

speaker_label: Professor DEBBIE WALSH (Director, Center for American Women in Politics, Rutgers' Eagleton Institute of Politics)
text: Right now, we have a record number of women who are serving as governors. But that's only nine women governors in this country. We have a record number of women in Congress overall, House and Senate, and that's only 16.3 percent of that institution.

speaker_label: Professor DEBBIE WALSH (Director, Center for American Women in Politics, Rutgers' Eagleton Institute of Politics)
text: We still aren't at anything close to parity. But we are seeing some of these significant accomplishments when we see women as the speaker of the U.S. House, and also women who are serving as speakers of the Houses and presidents of Senates across the country in state legislatures.

speaker_label: Professor DEBBIE WALSH (Director, Center for American Women in Politics, Rutgers' Eagleton Institute of Politics)
text: So we see women making breakthroughs. We see women making a difference when they're serving in office at all of these levels of government. But we still don't have enough women there, and I think a part of that is the system in which they're operating - a party system that doesn't necessarily reach out to women, doesn't encourage and support women in the same way that it does men. And I think that that has had an impact on the paucity of women in elective office.

We could not have this discussion without mentioning the name Senator Hillary Rodham Clinton, and let's do so now. What are some of the key obstacles - partisan issues aside, of course - facing the senator and her presidential ambition? And how do they differ, let's say, from other women who have run for president before her?

speaker_label: Professor DEBBIE WALSH (Director, Center for American Women in Politics, Rutgers' Eagleton Institute of Politics)
text: The last two women who ran for president of the United States -Elizabeth Dole and Carol Moseley Braun - both had to pull out of their races before even the first Iowa caucus or the New Hampshire primary. And it was because of money. Hillary Rodham Clinton won't face that challenge. She has tremendous name recognition, although I think in many ways - and she has said this herself - she is one of the best-known unknowns to the American public.

speaker_label: Professor DEBBIE WALSH (Director, Center for American Women in Politics, Rutgers' Eagleton Institute of Politics)
text: They have an image of her from her time as First Lady, but I think very few people in the American public have really focused on her as an elected woman in her own right. And now is the time that she will start to try to show the world and the voters in the United States who she is as a political person in her own right.

speaker_label: Professor DEBBIE WALSH (Director, Center for American Women in Politics, Rutgers' Eagleton Institute of Politics)
text: I think she faces some of the challenges of double standards that women face. I was noted that there have been some comments about her being ambitious, and having said that in a kind of a negative way that she's ambitious. And I stopped and wondered to think, you know, how many people could even think of running for president without being ambitious?

speaker_label: Professor DEBBIE WALSH (Director, Center for American Women in Politics, Rutgers' Eagleton Institute of Politics)
text: I'm sure every one of the men who is running for president, whether they're Democrats or Republican, are ambitious. But when it's said about a woman, somehow that has a negative connotation.
Take the rest of the world as part of our conversation. There are quite a few female leaders internationally. But what has kept America back?

speaker_label: Professor DEBBIE WALSH (Director, Center for American Women in Politics, Rutgers' Eagleton Institute of Politics)
text: I think that comes because of the number of reasons. One is, we have a different system than a lot of the countries that have elected women -parliamentary systems versus our system where the president is elected directly by the voters. And I think that makes - that changes it. And I think a lot of these other countries also have quotas when they run slates as candidates in these parliamentary systems.

speaker_label: Professor DEBBIE WALSH (Director, Center for American Women in Politics, Rutgers' Eagleton Institute of Politics)
text: There are a certain number of women that are required to be on the ballot. And as we all know in this country, if you say the Q word, people run fleeing. And so, I think that if the party has made a real commitment to electing women to office, I think we would have more women in elected office.

Here's another point. We've talked about external obstacles and male dominance in the political arena. How do you address the issue of self-perception of women and those self-perceptions that you think perhaps women need to overcome for themselves to increase their visibility in the political arena?

speaker_label: Professor DEBBIE WALSH (Director, Center for American Women in Politics, Rutgers' Eagleton Institute of Politics)
text: That's a really good question. We know that women are less likely to be what are called self-starters. You know, the people who wake up in the morning, look in the mirror and say, gosh, I'd be the best state senator or U.S. senator that my state has ever seen. Women are more likely to need to be asked to run, and by people who are within the political structure, sort of, telling them and encouraging them to do that.

speaker_label: Professor DEBBIE WALSH (Director, Center for American Women in Politics, Rutgers' Eagleton Institute of Politics)
text: And then we also know that if you look at the people who are in what are considered to be the potential pool of candidates - the professions like business and lawyers and teachers - when we ask people in those professions whether they have been asked to run for office, men are much more likely to be asked.

speaker_label: Professor DEBBIE WALSH (Director, Center for American Women in Politics, Rutgers' Eagleton Institute of Politics)
text: So you have a double whammy there. Women need to be asked, but they're not getting asked. So I think that's a real problem.
What role does a woman's race or ethnicity play in the way that she is perceived politically?

speaker_label: Professor DEBBIE WALSH (Director, Center for American Women in Politics, Rutgers' Eagleton Institute of Politics)
text: Yeah. I know that when Shirley Chisholm ran for president, you know, Shirley Chisholm didn't think she was going to win the presidency, but she felt a very strong obligation to show the American public that an African-American could run for the presidency of the United States and that a woman could run for president of the United States. And she wanted to be sure that there were issues raised that might not get raised, that probably certainly wouldn't get raised unless her voice was there speaking out, talking about those things. It was very important for her to be in the debates, and as many of those that she could be in.

speaker_label: Professor DEBBIE WALSH (Director, Center for American Women in Politics, Rutgers' Eagleton Institute of Politics)
text: And I think when women - when women of color - when people of color are running, I think that, you know, they have not been taken seriously. And I think that's why this year is such a breakthrough because we're seeing Barack Obama. We're seeing Governor Richardson. We're seeing Hillary Clinton. We're seeing the range of folks expanding beyond white men, and those people are being taken seriously. And I think that's really a breakthrough.
Debbie Walsh, thank you very much - a very interesting conversation.

speaker_label: Professor DEBBIE WALSH (Director, Center for American Women in Politics, Rutgers' Eagleton Institute of Politics)
text: Thank you. I enjoyed it.

Debbie Walsh is director of the Center for American Women and Politics at Rutgers Eagleton Institute of Politics. To hear an extended version of our conversation and to keep tabs on our "Leading Ladies" series, visit the NEWS & NOTES page at npr.org.
